turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. Um, honestly, I'm just... I'm really struggling right now to get anything done. Since I'm not working right now, I've been trying to focus on, you know, getting my life together, filling out job applications and stuff. Which is already tough enough since I just have my high school diploma, so I really need to put the effort in, but... well, the main thing is I just get pulled completely off track by every little sound or thought. 

It's actually ridiculous. I'll sit down at my laptop, right? I'll be trying to work on an application, maybe I'm typing in my past experience or trying to answer one of those questionnaire things, and then a car will drive by outside—just a normal car, nothing special, maybe the muffler is a bit loud—and suddenly I'm looking out the window, wondering where they're going or thinking about traffic. Or my phone screen will light up with a notification, not even a text, just like a spam email or a weather alert, and I just have to pick it up. 

Or even worse, it's not even something around me, just some random idea pops into my head. Like I'll suddenly wonder if I need to buy more paper towels, or I'll remember a movie I saw five years ago, and it just sends me somewhere else entirely. And the crazy part is, I don't even notice it happening. Like, an hour will go by, and I'm deep into some internet rabbit hole about, I don't know, how they build suspension bridges, and the job application is just sitting there completely blank. It's just so frustrating because I really *want* to finish it, I sit down with every intention of finishing it, but my brain just won't stay put, you know? It's like every little thing completely hijacks my attention and I just can't filter it out.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain attention on tasks like filling out job applications, noting that their brain 'won't stay put' and tasks remain unfinished.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly states they are easily distracted by extraneous stimuli like cars outside or phone notifications, as well as unrelated thoughts popping into their head.

turns.doctor_question: When you get distracted by these things—like the car noise or the random thoughts—are you usually worried or anxious about something, or does your mind just jump to them without any particular worry attached?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, it's definitely not a worry thing. I mean, don't get me wrong, being unemployed is stressful, obviously, and I do stress about that in general, but in that exact moment when the car drives by? I'm not sitting there panicking about my life or feeling anxious or anything like that. It's literally just... zip, my brain is over there now. 

Like, there's zero anxiety attached to the actual distraction. Take the paper towel thing I just mentioned. When I think about the paper towels, I'm not sitting there like, "Oh my god, what if I spill something and I don't have anything to wipe it up with, what a complete disaster!" It's nothing like that. It's more just a completely neutral, random observation that suddenly feels like the absolute most important thing in the world to figure out right that second. Like my brain just changes the channel without asking me and suddenly I'm watching a completely different show. 

I could be totally relaxed, you know, maybe drinking a cup of coffee, feeling pretty good about the morning, not a worry in the world, and then I'll see, I don't know, a weird bug on the windowsill. And suddenly I'm just looking at the bug. I'm not worried about the bug biting me, I'm not scared of it, I'm just looking at its legs, wondering how it climbs the glass, trying to remember what kind of bugs live in this area. So yeah, to answer your question, it's not anxiety. It's just... my attention gets completely hijacked by whatever shiny new thing enters my orbit, whether it's a sound or a thought or whatever, completely out of nowhere, and worry has nothing to do with it.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient confirms their attention is easily hijacked by extraneous stimuli like sounds, bugs, or random thoughts.
symptom_reasoning.S062: The patient explicitly denies being scared of or worried about the bug they get distracted by.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been experiencing this difficulty with concentration and distractibility? Did this start when you were younger, or is this something that's more recent?
turns.patient_response:
Well, see, that's the thing. I mean, I guess I've always been a little scatterbrained, you know? Like in high school, I wasn't exactly the star pupil sitting in the front row taking perfect notes. But it was never... it was never *this* bad. This whole level of just complete inability to stay on track, where it's actually ruining my day and keeping me from getting a job? That really kicked into high gear about, I'd say, a year and ten months ago. 

Yeah, almost exactly a year and ten months, because that's when I had this really bad soccer injury. I used to play in this adult rec league, right? Just a casual thing, but we played hard, and I ended up completely tearing my ACL. It was awful. I had to have surgery, and the recovery was just brutal. I was basically stuck on the couch for weeks, and then I had months of physical therapy. 

And before that, I had a really solid routine. I was working, I was playing soccer three nights a week, I was going to the gym on the off days... I was always moving. Always burning off energy, always having somewhere I needed to be at a specific time. But when the injury happened, all of that just stopped. Completely stopped. Suddenly I had zero structure, zero physical outlet, and it was like my brain just didn't know what to do with itself. 

I thought once I healed up, things would go back to normal, but they just... didn't. Even after I could walk fine again, the routine was gone, the job was gone, and this crazy distractibility just stayed. It's like the injury knocked me out of my orbit, and I've just been floating around in space ever since, unable to latch onto anything for more than five minutes. So yeah, I'd say it's been about a year and ten months of it being this disruptive.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes a 'complete inability to stay on track' and being 'unable to latch onto anything for more than five minutes,' indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly mentions experiencing 'crazy distractibility' and describes themselves as having always been 'scatterbrained.'

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned you used to be very active—playing soccer, going to the gym, always moving around. Since your injury and losing that routine, have you noticed that you feel restless or fidgety a lot? Like, do you find yourself tapping your feet, bouncing your leg, or feeling like you need to move around, even when you're trying to sit still and focus?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. Yeah, 100%. It's actually kind of funny you mention that because my buddy was just getting onto me about it the other day. Like, whenever I'm sitting down, especially if I'm sitting with someone else, my leg is just going a mile a minute. Just constantly bouncing up and down. I don't even know I'm doing it until the whole table starts shaking and whoever I'm with is like, "Dude, chill out," and they have to literally put their hand on my knee to get me to stop. 

And if it's not my leg doing the bouncing, it's my hands. I literally cannot keep my hands empty. If I'm trying to sit still, I'll be clicking a pen—just click, click, click, click—driving everyone in the room crazy. Or I'll have my hand in my pocket just messing with my keys, jingling them around. I have this one keychain, it's like this metal bottle opener thing from my old soccer team, and I'll just sit there flipping it over and over in my fingers without even realizing I'm doing it. 

It's exactly like you said, it's like because I'm not running up and down a field anymore, all that physical energy just got trapped inside my body and it has to leak out somehow, you know? Like a pressure valve or something. So I'm just constantly fidgeting. Even when I'm trying to do those job applications I was telling you about earlier, I'll have a pen in one hand just spinning it or clicking it while I'm trying to read the screen, which obviously doesn't help me focus at all. I just... I don't even realize it's happening. It's completely unconscious. I'll be sitting there, thinking I'm being perfectly relaxed and still, and then I look down and my leg is practically vibrating off the floor. 

It's just so weird how your body does things without your brain giving the okay, right? Like, I'll be at a coffee shop—well, not so much lately since I'm trying to save money since I'm not working, but you know what I mean. If I'm anywhere where I have to just sit and be normal, the bouncing and the clicking and the key jingling just starts up completely on its own.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly describes constantly bouncing their leg, clicking pens, and playing with keys while seated.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes feeling like physical energy is trapped inside their body like a pressure valve, indicating a strong sense of internal restlessness.

turns.doctor_question: Going back to elementary school and middle school, before high school even—do you remember having trouble paying attention in class, or were teachers ever concerned about you being fidgety or restless back then?
turns.patient_response:
Oh man, elementary school. Yeah. I mean, I know I said earlier that I was scatterbrained in high school, but honestly, if I really think about it, it goes way, way back before that. 

Like, even back in second or third grade, I remember my teachers were just constantly—and I mean *constantly*—moving my seat around the classroom. It was almost like a running joke, except the teachers definitely weren't laughing. They'd start me out in the middle of the room, right? Sitting with a group of desks. But I just could not keep my mouth shut. If a thought popped into my head, I'd just say it out loud, right in the middle of the lesson. I'd just blurt things out, completely out of turn, or I'd be whispering to whoever was sitting next to me about some cartoon I saw or whatever. So then the teacher would sigh and move my desk to the front row. But then I'd just talk to the teacher! So then they'd move me to the very back corner, away from everyone else. 

And it wasn't just the talking, either. It was the homework. Oh man, my backpack was just this absolute black hole of crumpled up papers. I would just completely forget I even had homework. I'd get to school and everyone's turning in their folders and I'm just sitting there like, "Wait, we had something to do?" My mom used to get so frustrated because the teachers were always sending home these little notes about missing assignments. 

And then when we actually had to do work in class—like, you know those worksheets they'd give you? The ones with like fifty little math problems on them, or the spelling words? I would just blast through them. I just wanted to be done. I couldn't stand just sitting there working on it slowly, so I'd rush through the whole page in like two minutes flat. And then the teacher would hand it back the next day and it would just be covered in red ink. And the frustrating part was, it wasn't because I didn't know the material! It was just completely careless mistakes. Like, I'd write a plus sign instead of a minus, or I'd just completely skip an entire row of questions because my eyes jumped down the page too fast and I didn't even notice. 

So yeah, they were always trying to find the "perfect" spot in the room to put my desk where I'd magically stop talking and actually remember my work and slow down, but it never really mattered where they put me. I was always just rushing through those worksheets and making a mess of things. I had this one teacher, Mrs. Gable in third grade, she actually taped a little square on the floor right next to her own desk and that was my spot for like half the year because I was just so all over the place... so yeah, it definitely started way back then, for sure.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient describes rushing through worksheets and making careless mistakes, such as skipping rows or using the wrong math sign.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes their backpack as a 'black hole of crumpled up papers,' indicating difficulty with organization.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient reports completely forgetting they had homework and frequently having missing assignments.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient states they 'could not keep my mouth shut' and would constantly talk during class.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly mentions blurting things out completely out of turn during lessons.

turns.doctor_question: When you think back to those early years—second, third grade—do you remember if you were bouncing your leg, fidgeting with things in your hands, or having that restless energy even back then, or did that physical restlessness develop later on?
turns.patient_response:
You know, it’s funny you ask that, because I’ve been thinking about it... back in second or third grade, I don't actually remember doing the whole leg-bouncing or the pen-clicking thing. But I think... well, I think that’s just because back then, I was always allowed to just run around, you know? You had recess, you had gym class, you rode your bike around the neighborhood until the streetlights came on. I was always just moving my whole body, so the energy never really got backed up, if that makes sense? 

But this current thing, this intense physical restlessness I have right now? That definitely feels like it developed later. Or, well, specifically after the injury. Because, like I was saying, since I can't play soccer like before, that energy is just completely trapped. Sitting around the house makes me feel like I’m literally crawling out of my skin. It’s this horrible, buzzing feeling right under the surface, and I just can't take it, so I end up pacing from room to room. 

I mean, I'll just walk from the living room to the kitchen, open the fridge, stare at the ketchup bottle for ten seconds, close it, walk down the hall, look out the bedroom window, and then walk right back to the kitchen. Just doing laps in my own house. My buddy came over the other day to hang out and he actually asked if I was waiting for a package or something because I just could not sit down on the couch with him to watch TV. I just kept pacing back and forth behind the sofa. It's like I'm a caged animal at the zoo or something. 

So yeah, the childhood stuff was more just me being a loud kid who couldn't shut up or stay in his seat, but this crawling-out-of-my-skin, pacing-the-floors kind of restlessness? That's all from losing soccer, 100 percent. I just don't know what to do with my own body anymore when I'm just supposed to be relaxing at home.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states that during childhood, he was a kid who 'couldn't stay in his seat.'
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an intense physical restlessness, feeling like he is 'crawling out of his skin,' and constantly pacing around the house.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient mentions that in childhood he was a loud kid who 'couldn't shut up.'
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies remembering doing any leg-bouncing or pen-clicking (fidgeting) during his childhood.

turns.doctor_question: When you were in high school—before the soccer injury—did you still have that same trouble focusing on homework and tests, or had things improved by that point?
turns.patient_response:
High school... man, high school is honestly kind of a blur when I try to think about the actual school part of it. Like I said before, I was definitely scatterbrained, but if you're asking if the homework and the tests specifically got better or worse... I really don't know. I can't even picture myself sitting at a desk doing homework back then. 

Because, see, by the time I hit high school, my entire existence—and I mean literally everything I did from the second I woke up to the second I went to sleep—was just completely wrapped up in soccer. We had morning conditioning, then regular classes, then afternoon practice, and then usually film review or something after that. So my brain was just... it was 100 percent on the sport. 

I honestly couldn't tell you if my focus in class improved, or if I just sort of figured out how to fly under the radar, you know? Like, the teachers all knew who I was because I was on varsity, and the coaches were always checking our grades to make sure we were eligible to play. So I just did whatever the absolute bare minimum was to keep my GPA exactly where it needed to be. I'd get home at like seven or eight at night, completely dead on my feet, my mom would have this massive plate of food waiting for me—usually pasta or something heavy because of all the calories I was burning—and I'd just eat and pass out. 

I don't remember having those same moments of sitting there rushing through fifty math problems like I did in third grade, but I also don't remember ever actually sitting down and studying for a history test, either. I would just kind of show up, stare at the clock, and wait for the bell to ring so I could get back out to the locker room. 

So... yeah, I don't really have a good answer for you on that one. I'm not sure if the trouble focusing went away, or if I just didn't care enough about the classes to even notice I wasn't focusing, if that makes sense? I was just surviving the school day until practice started.

turns.doctor_question: Let me ask about middle school specifically—do you remember having trouble keeping up with assignments, or did your teachers ever send notes home about incomplete work or you not paying attention in class back then?
turns.patient_response:
Middle school... man, that's kind of a weird time to try and remember. Sixth, seventh, eighth grade... you know, it's funny, because elementary school is just so vivid in my mind with the whole desk-moving thing, and then high school, like I was just saying, was just pure, one-hundred-percent soccer. But middle school is kind of this weird, blurry gray area in the middle. 

I mean, that's the age when everything changes, right? You're not just in one room all day with one teacher who watches your every move. Suddenly you have, like, six different teachers for different subjects, and you have to navigate the crowded hallways, and you have to remember your locker combination—which, by the way, I was absolutely terrible at. I was always that kid yanking on the metal handle and having to go find the janitor to cut the lock or look up my combination because I just couldn't keep the numbers in my head. 

But as for the actual assignments, or teachers sending notes home about me not paying attention... I honestly couldn't tell you. I just don't have a clear memory of it one way or the other. I mean, I probably was missing things? But I don't remember my mom getting those little physical notes like she did back in third grade. I think maybe by middle school, teachers just don't really send notes home the same way, you know? They expect you to be more independent. 

Or maybe... well, I remember they made us buy those planner things. Do you remember those? The school would hand out these little spiral-bound agendas with the school mascot on the front, and they'd tell you to write all your homework down every single day. I would always start off the year with the absolute best intentions. Like, the first week of sixth grade, I'd be writing everything down, maybe even using different colored pens for math and science, really trying to stay on top of it. But then by, like, the second week of October, that planner is just completely buried at the bottom of my locker underneath a bunch of gym shirts and crushed up Doritos bags. 

But yeah, specifically remembering if I was falling behind on assignments or getting called out in class back then... I really just draw a blank. It all just blends together into this awkward phase where I was just trying to figure out how the bells worked and getting really involved in club soccer outside of school. So I don't really have a specific answer for you on the middle school stuff.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes severe disorganization, noting that their school planner would quickly end up buried at the bottom of a messy locker.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient reports being forgetful in daily school activities, specifically being unable to remember their locker combination and needing the janitor to cut the lock.

turns.doctor_question: When you think back to middle school and high school, before the soccer injury—aside from just being busy with soccer—do you remember ever getting in trouble with teachers for talking out of turn, or forgetting to turn in assignments, or making careless mistakes on tests the way you did back in elementary school?
turns.patient_response:
I know you're trying to piece together that timeline, and I really wish I could give you a better picture, but... I just draw a complete blank on that specific stuff. Like, I genuinely don't remember getting in trouble for talking out of turn or anything like that once I got older. I mean, maybe I did? But if it happened, it definitely didn't stick in my brain the way the elementary school stuff did. 

You have to remember, by the time you're in high school, the whole dynamic is just completely different. In third grade, you've got one teacher who is basically hovering over you all day, watching every single thing you do. But in high school? You're just one of, like, thirty kids in a room, and honestly, half the teachers looked like they were just trying to survive until the bell rang, too. I would usually just find a desk way in the back row—ideally near the window or the radiator, because I was always freezing after our morning conditioning sessions—and I would just try to be invisible. I wasn't really the loud, disruptive kid anymore because I was just so physically exhausted all the time. When you're running sprints at six in the morning, you don't really have the energy to be talking out of turn in second-period history, you know? I was practically sleeping with my eyes open.

And as for the careless mistakes on tests or forgetting assignments... I mean, I don't have any specific memories of a teacher pulling me aside to lecture me about it. They didn't really do that anymore. If I messed up on a test, they'd just hand it back with a red C-minus scribbled on the top and move on to the next kid. And with the missing assignments, it was all just a hustle to stay eligible for the team. If a teacher warned me I was missing something, I'd just scramble and copy a worksheet from one of my teammates in the cafeteria right before class. It was never this big sit-down intervention. 

So, yeah, I just... I don't remember any of that happening in middle or high school. I wasn't getting called out, I wasn't getting in trouble... or at least, if I was, I have absolutely zero memory of it. It was all just about doing the bare minimum to get through the hallway and get back out on the field.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient admits to having missing assignments in high school, noting they would scramble to copy a teammate's worksheet when warned by a teacher.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient describes being 'physically exhausted all the time' and 'practically sleeping with my eyes open' due to morning conditioning sessions.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient explicitly states they were not 'the loud, disruptive kid anymore' in high school.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient denies remembering talking out of turn or being disruptive during middle and high school.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient denies talking out of turn or being a loud, disruptive kid who interrupted class.

turns.doctor_question: I want to go back to high school for a second. Even though you were exhausted from soccer, do you remember struggling to focus during class or on tests back then—like, did you find your mind wandering, or did you have to re-read things multiple times because you weren't paying attention, even when you weren't tired?
turns.patient_response:
Man, high school... like I said, it's just really hard to separate what was me being physically exhausted from what was just my brain not working right. I'm sure I probably did have to re-read stuff in class, but I just don't have a specific memory of sitting at a desk and doing it back then. 

But, I mean, if you're talking about that specific feeling—where your mind just wanders off and you have to go back over things—I do that constantly right now. Like, all the time. And it's not even with boring school stuff or when I'm tired, it's with things I actually *want* to be doing, when I'm wide awake. 

For example, I like to try and fix things, right? So I can start watching a repair video on YouTube, one of those step-by-step tutorials, or I'll sit down to read the manual for a new tool I just got. I'm genuinely trying to figure out how to use the thing so I don't break it. But after a few minutes, I'll suddenly sort of... snap back to reality, and I realize I've just been staring blankly at it. Like, my eyes are on the screen, the guy in the video is talking, but my brain is completely somewhere else. I haven't processed a single word for the last five minutes. My mind just completely drifted off to something else entirely—like what I'm going to eat later, or some random thought about a car I saw on the street. 

So then I have to stop, grab my phone or the mouse, and back the video up because absolutely none of it stuck. And the crazy part is, sometimes I'll rewind it, start playing it again, and then I'll zone out at the exact same spot! I'll have to rewind the same two-minute clip like three or four times just to get through one step of the repair. It's so frustrating because I'm sitting there thinking, "Come on, just pay attention to this one simple thing," but it's like trying to hold water in your hands. It just slips right through. 

So yeah, I might not remember doing it with a biology textbook in tenth grade because of the whole soccer blur, but I definitely do exactly what you're talking about with repair videos and manuals today. It just doesn't stay in my head.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly describes an inability to sustain attention on tasks like watching repair videos or reading manuals, frequently zoning out and having to rewind or re-read.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient mentions being distracted by unrelated thoughts, such as thinking about what to eat or a random car on the street, while trying to focus on a task.

turns.doctor_question: I know you can't remember every detail, but let me ask you this: Did your parents or teachers ever express concern about your grades or your ability to keep up academically in middle school, even before soccer became such a big part of your life?
turns.patient_response:
Man, you are really digging into the middle school vault today. Grades... okay, let me try to think about report cards back then. We used to get them mailed directly to the house at the end of every quarter, and they always came in those little white window envelopes. I remember my mom would usually be the one to open them because she always grabbed the mail from the box at the end of the driveway first thing. She would stand in the kitchen, usually right by the landline phone—we had this massive, ridiculously long curly cord on it that could stretch all the way across the room to the fridge—and she would open the envelope right there. 

But as for her actually expressing concern, or my dad sitting me down because I wasn't keeping up? I just don't think so. Or at least, I have zero memory of it. I feel like if I was totally bombing out and failing my classes, I would definitely remember the fallout from that, right? Like, you remember getting grounded or losing your privileges. I had a PlayStation 2 back then, and I played it constantly, so if they had taken that away because of my grades, that would be burned into my brain. But I don't remember any big, dramatic interventions or them telling me I needed a tutor or anything like that. 

And with the teachers, it was kind of a different vibe than elementary school. That was the first time we had to switch rooms for every subject, so instead of one teacher who knew everything about you, you were just one of like thirty kids cycling through their room for forty-five minutes. So maybe I was just flying under the radar. Maybe I was just pulling solid C-minuses and blending in with the background, so nobody felt the need to sound the alarm. I really don't remember any teacher ever holding me after the bell rang to tell me they were worried about my academic progress. If they did, or if my parents were secretly stressing out about it behind closed doors, they kept it from me, because I just don't have any memory of anyone being concerned about it back then.

turns.doctor_question: I want to make sure I understand the timeline correctly. You've told me that in elementary school—second, third grade—you were definitely fidgety, talking out of turn, and making careless mistakes on worksheets. But when you think back to that time, do you also remember your mind wandering or getting distracted from your schoolwork the way it does now with those job applications—where you lose an hour to something completely unrelated?
turns.patient_response:
Well, when you compare it to the job applications... I mean, the way it happens now is just so frustrating, because the main thing is I get pulled off track by every little sound or thought. It’s like I have zero filter for the rest of the world. I’ll be sitting there at my laptop, trying to work on an application—typing in my address, trying to remember the exact months I worked at my last job—and then a car will drive by outside. Not even a loud car, just tires on the wet pavement. Or my phone will vibrate on the desk, or, honestly, it doesn't even have to be a real sound. It could just be some random idea that pops into my head, like wondering if I left my wet towel on the bed or trying to remember the name of an actor from a movie I watched three weeks ago. And that just sends me somewhere else entirely before I even notice it's happening. I don't make a conscious choice to stop working on the application, I just suddenly snap back to reality and realize I've been watching YouTube videos about restoring old cast iron skillets for an hour. 

But back in second or third grade? Did I do that? I mean, obviously I wasn't falling down internet rabbit holes, but... yeah, I think the actual feeling of it was exactly the same. 

I remember my third-grade classroom had those individual desks that the teacher would push together into little groups of four or five, you know, to make little pods? And if we were supposed to be doing a spelling worksheet, I wouldn't be doing it, because I'd hear the radiator clanking by the window. Or someone across the room would get up to use the pencil sharpener—one of those old, heavy metal crank ones bolted to the wall that made that awful grinding noise—and my brain would just instantly lock onto that sound. Then I'd be watching them sharpen the pencil, and then I'd look past them out the window at the playground, and I'd start thinking about recess, and I'd just be completely gone in my own head. 

So I wasn't losing an hour to a phone, because I didn't have one, but I was definitely getting hijacked by every little distraction in that classroom before I even realized I wasn't doing my work. The teacher would say time was up, and I'd look down, and I had maybe written my name at the top of the paper. So yeah, the stuff distracting me has changed, but that immediate pull away from whatever I'm supposed to be focusing on? That was definitely happening back then, too.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes a chronic inability to sustain attention on tasks like job applications or school worksheets, often losing focus for long periods.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient recalls failing to finish schoolwork, noting that when time was up for a worksheet, they had often only written their name.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly confirms being easily pulled off track by extraneous stimuli, such as minor sounds or unrelated thoughts, both currently and during childhood.
